templates.principle: Peak-end — the highest-effort note in the system lands three days after the sale, while the memory is still warm
templates.subject: the {vehicle} and my number
templates.emailBody: {first}, thank you for buying the {vehicle} from me. Save this number in your phone as Mick at Mosaic, {phone}, and if anything feels off in the first couple weeks, call me before you call anybody else. The title and plates come through the state, not me, so if they feel slow that is normal, and if they feel too slow, tell me and I will chase it. I am glad it was you sitting across the desk. Okay if I send you a note every few months with seasonal stuff worth knowing about the {vehicle}?
templates.textBody: {first}, this is Mick at Mosaic, save this number, and call me first if anything on the {vehicle} feels off. Okay if I send you a note every few months with seasonal stuff worth knowing about the {vehicle}?
templates.editHint: Add one detail from the sale day (the dog, the kid, what they traded) so it reads like memory, not a form.

templates.principle: Peak-end — gratitude plus a real promise of access, before any ask
templates.subject: glad it was you
templates.emailBody: Thanks again, {first}, for trusting me with the {vehicle}. Handing somebody the keys and then never hearing from them again is not how I want to do this, so my number is {phone} and it goes straight to me, not a front desk. Plates and title come from the state on their own clock, and I will nudge if they drag. If a light comes on or something sounds different than it did on the test drive, call me and we will figure out whether it is a nothing or a something. Okay if I send you a note now and then with seasonal stuff worth knowing about the {vehicle}?
templates.textBody: Thanks again for trusting me with the {vehicle}, {first}, and my number goes straight to me, so call if anything sounds different. Okay if I send you a note now and then with seasonal stuff worth knowing about the {vehicle}?
templates.editHint: If they already mentioned a noise or a worry on the test drive, name it in the fourth sentence.

templates.principle: Peak-end and consistency — restates what they said they needed, so the relationship starts on their words
templates.subject: one thing before you forget
templates.emailBody: {first}, before the {vehicle} turns into just the thing you drive, put this number in your phone under Mick at Mosaic, {phone}. Here is why I ask: the first few weeks are when a small noise or a dash light shows up, and I would rather hear about it from you than have you wonder who to call. The title and plates come from the state and not from me, so give them a bit before you worry. You told me what you needed this rig to do, and I want to hear whether it is doing it. Okay if I send you a note every few months with seasonal stuff worth knowing about the {vehicle}?
templates.textBody: {first}, put this number in your phone as Mick at Mosaic, and if the {vehicle} makes a noise it did not make on the test drive, I want the call. Okay if I send you a note every few months with seasonal stuff worth knowing about the {vehicle}?
templates.editHint: Replace 'what you needed this rig to do' with the actual job they told you about (hauling, the Rochester commute, a kid's first car).

templates.principle: Peak-end — one useful housekeeping tip, one warm line, one honest consent question
templates.subject: your {model} and how to find me
templates.emailBody: It was good doing business with you, {first}. Two housekeeping things: my number is {phone}, and the title and plates come through the state, so if the mailbox is quiet for a while, that is them and not me. Keep the paperwork somewhere you can find it, because the day you need it is never the day you remember where it went. You bought a good one and I am glad it went home with you. Okay if I send a note every few months with seasonal stuff worth knowing about the {vehicle}?
templates.textBody: Good doing business with you, {first}, and this is the number to use if anything comes up with the {vehicle}. Okay if I send a note every few months with seasonal stuff worth knowing about the {vehicle}?
templates.editHint: If you handed them a folder or an extra key, say so in the paperwork line.

templates.principle: Consistency and identity — names the repeat out loud so they see themselves as someone who comes back
templates.subject: round two
templates.emailBody: {first}, twice now, and I do not take that lightly. Thank you for coming back for the {vehicle} instead of driving to Rochester to start over with a stranger. Same rules as last time: my number is {phone}, plates and title come from the state on their own schedule, and if anything feels off early, I want the call. The notes I send will switch over to this one so you are not getting winter tips for a rig you no longer own. Still okay with me sending you a note every few months about the {vehicle}?
templates.textBody: {first}, twice now, and thank you for coming back for the {vehicle} instead of starting over with a stranger. Still okay with me sending you a note every few months about the {vehicle}?
templates.editHint: Name the first vehicle in the second sentence if you remember it ('after the Equinox').

templates.principle: Peak-end — gratitude that a second purchase is the only review that matters, no ask beyond consent
templates.subject: welcome back
templates.emailBody: Welcome back, {first}. A second one from the same guy says more about the first one than any review ever could, and I am grateful for it. The {vehicle} paperwork will come from the state the same as last time, and my number is still {phone} if a light or a noise shows up early. I will point the seasonal notes at the new rig from here on. Still good with a note from me every few months about the {vehicle}?
templates.textBody: Welcome back, {first}, and thank you for coming back for the {vehicle}, which means more to me than any review. Still good with a note from me every few months about the {vehicle}?
templates.editHint: If a family member drove the first one, mention who is driving this one.

templates.principle: Reciprocity, honestly earned — a real road warning for the exact roads they drive, no pitch
templates.subject: deer on 52 at dusk
templates.emailBody: {first}, the deer are moving hard from now through the rut, and dusk to a couple hours after dark is when they cross Hwy 52 and Hwy 58 down by the river bottoms. If you see one, assume there are two more behind it, brake straight, and do not swerve into the ditch or the oncoming lane, because the ditch and the oncoming lane both hurt worse than the deer. Slow down where the corn just came out, since they have lost their cover and are crossing to find more. If you do hit one, pull over, put the flashers on, and call the county before you call me. Do you drive that stretch after dark much?
templates.textBody: {first}, deer are moving hard along Hwy 52 and Hwy 58 at dusk, so brake straight and never swerve, and figure there are two more behind the first one. Do you drive that stretch after dark much?
templates.editHint: Swap the highway for the road they actually drive home on (the hook field is a good source).

templates.principle: Reciprocity — a diagnostic question that helps them notice their own battery before January does
templates.subject: the battery and the first cold snap
templates.emailBody: Quick one, {first}. The first hard cold morning of the year is when a tired battery quits, and it always picks the morning you have somewhere to be. Any parts store or shop will load test it for nothing while you wait, and it takes about as long as pumping gas. If the {vehicle} has been cranking a hair slower than it did in August, that is the battery telling you something before it says it louder in January. Has the {vehicle} been turning over a little slow lately?
templates.textBody: {first}, the first cold snap is when a tired battery quits, and any parts store will load test it while you wait. Has the {vehicle} been turning over a little slow lately?
templates.editHint: If you know the battery was new at the sale, say so and change the question to whether the cables are tight.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — the penny test and a wiper check, the same list Mick runs on his own truck
templates.subject: tires before the first snow
templates.emailBody: {first}, before the first real snow lands on Hwy 58, it is worth a minute with a penny and your tires. Stick it in the tread upside down, and if you can see the whole head, the tread is too low to bite in slush, which is what you find on the hill into Zumbrota in November. While you are down there, look at the wiper blades, because the first wet snow shows you real quick which ones are shot. None of this is a pitch, it is just the stuff I check on my own truck every October. Is the {vehicle} still on the tires it came with?
templates.textBody: {first}, penny in the tread before the first snow, and if you can see the whole head the tires will not bite in slush. Is the {vehicle} still on the tires it came with?
templates.editHint: If you put new tires on it at the sale, change the question to whether they have rotated them yet.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — a five-minute headlight check anyone can do in a driveway
templates.subject: headlights and shorter days
templates.emailBody: {first}, the sun is going down before supper now, and headlights that are aimed low or fogged over turn a deer on Hwy 52 into a surprise instead of a warning. Park facing a garage door or a wall at night and look at the two beams, because if one is noticeably lower or dimmer than the other, that is aim or a bulb, and both are quick fixes. If the lenses have gone yellow and hazy, a headlight restoring kit from the parts store and twenty minutes gets you real light back. Clean the inside of the windshield too, since the film that builds up there is half the reason oncoming lights feel so bright. Have you noticed the {vehicle} lighting up the road less than it used to?
templates.textBody: {first}, days are short now, so park facing a wall tonight and look at your two headlight beams, and if one is low or dim, that is a quick fix. Have you noticed the {vehicle} lighting up the road less than it used to?
templates.editHint: Older rigs get the hazy-lens line; newer ones can drop it and keep the aim check.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — block heater cord check and a plug-in timing rule, before the twenty-below week
templates.subject: block heater and the cold-start morning
templates.emailBody: {first}, if the {vehicle} has a block heater, now is when it earns its keep, and the cord is the part that fails first. Pull it out, look for cracks or a melted plug end, and if it looks rough, replace the cord before the twenty-below week, not during it. Plug in for two or three hours before you leave, not all night, since a timer on the outlet does that for you. If it does not have one, a battery blanket or just parking nose-in out of the wind makes a real difference on the cold mornings. Does the {vehicle} have a block heater?
templates.textBody: {first}, if the {vehicle} has a block heater, check the cord for cracks now and plug in a few hours before you leave, not all night. Does the {vehicle} have a block heater?
templates.editHint: If you know it has one (diesel, or you saw the cord), change the question to whether it is plugged in on the cold nights.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — explains what a slow crank means so they can decide for themselves, no urgency invented
templates.subject: what a slow crank is telling you
templates.emailBody: {first}, here is the thing about a slow crank on a cold morning: it is the {vehicle} telling you the battery is working near its limit, and cold cuts a battery's strength almost in half. If it groans for a second before it catches, that is a warning, and if it just clicks, the warning is over. Any parts store will test it for nothing, and if it is more than four winters old, it is living on borrowed time whether or not it has complained yet. I would rather you hear it from me in January than from a tow truck driver in a parking lot in Rochester. Has the {vehicle} been groaning before it catches?
templates.textBody: {first}, a slow groan before the {vehicle} catches on a cold morning is the battery near its limit, and any parts store will test it while you wait. Has the {vehicle} been groaning before it catches?
templates.editHint: If the fall battery note already went to this customer, swap the parts-store line for the cable-corrosion check.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — salt and tire pressure explained plainly, so the low tire light stops being a mystery
templates.subject: salt, tire pressure, and the cold
templates.emailBody: Two small winter things for the {vehicle}, {first}. The county salts Hwy 52 heavy and the brine sits underneath eating brake lines until spring, so on a day above freezing, run it through a wash with the undercarriage spray, even if washing a truck in January looks silly. Tire pressure also drops about a pound for every ten degrees the temperature falls, so if the low tire light came on the first cold morning, that is probably all it is, and a gas station air hose fixes it. Check all four and the spare while you are at it, since the spare is the one everybody forgets. Has that low tire light come on yet this winter?
templates.textBody: {first}, tire pressure drops about a pound for every ten degrees, so a low tire light on a cold morning is usually just air, and an undercarriage wash on a mild day gets the salt off before it eats the brake lines. Has that low tire light come on yet this winter?
templates.editHint: If they drive gravel more than highway, cut the salt line down and keep the tire pressure part.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — the ditch kit, the half-tank rule, and stay-with-the-rig, from someone who has been in the ditch
templates.subject: the ditch kit
templates.emailBody: {first}, if you go in the ditch on Hwy 58 in a whiteout, help is coming, but it may be a while. Keep a blanket, a candle and lighter, a phone cord, a bag of sand, and a small shovel behind the seat of the {vehicle}. If you do go in, stay with the rig, since a running engine and a cracked window beat walking every time. One rule I tell everybody: keep the tank above half from December on, because a full tank keeps the fuel line from freezing and keeps you warm if you are stuck. Is there a blanket in the {vehicle} right now?
templates.textBody: {first}, blanket, candle, phone cord, sand, and a small shovel behind the seat, and keep the tank above half from December on. Is there a blanket in the {vehicle} right now?
templates.editHint: For a car instead of a truck, change 'behind the seat' to 'in the trunk' and drop the shovel if it will not fit.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — where Minnesota rust starts and how to get the salt off before it does
templates.subject: get the salt off
templates.emailBody: {first}, the snow is finally gone off Hwy 52 and now the salt gets to work on the {vehicle} for real, because it eats faster when it is wet and warm than when it is frozen. First mild weekend, run it through a wash with the undercarriage spray, or put a lawn sprinkler under it for twenty minutes, which sounds dumb and works fine. Pay attention to the rocker panels behind the wheels and the seams where the bed or trunk meets the body, since that is where Minnesota rust starts. Wash the floor mats out too, since the salt off your boots does the same thing to the floor pan from the inside. Got the salt off the {vehicle} yet this spring?
templates.textBody: {first}, the salt eats faster once it warms up, so first mild weekend give the {vehicle} an undercarriage wash and hose the mats out. Got the salt off the {vehicle} yet this spring?
templates.editHint: Say 'bed' for a truck, 'trunk' for a car, and drop the one that does not apply.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — a self-test for alignment they can run on the way home, no appointment implied
templates.subject: potholes and a crooked wheel
templates.emailBody: {first}, after a winter of potholes on Hwy 58, here is a quick test that tells you a lot: on a flat straight stretch, loosen your grip and see whether the {vehicle} drifts, and look at whether the steering wheel sits straight when you are going straight. A pull or a crooked wheel usually means the alignment got knocked out, and driving on it chews the inside edge off a tire before you ever notice. A shimmy in the wheel around highway speed is more often a bent rim or a lost wheel weight than anything scary. None of it is an emergency, but all of it is easier on the tires the sooner it gets set right. Does the {vehicle} pull to one side when you let go of the wheel?
templates.textBody: {first}, after a winter of potholes, loosen your grip on a straight stretch and see if the {vehicle} drifts, because a pull chews a tire edge fast. Does the {vehicle} pull to one side when you let go of the wheel?
templates.editHint: Name the pothole stretch they complain about if you know it (the hook field, or the road into their place).

templates.principle: Reciprocity — hail parking and a brake-noise explanation, both things people quietly worry about
templates.subject: hail season and where you park
templates.emailBody: {first}, hail season starts up around here in May, and the storms that come up the Zumbro valley late in the afternoon do not give much warning. If the sky turns that green color, the {vehicle} is better off under a gas station canopy or in a garage than on the south side of the house, and if you are caught out in it, pull well off the road and point the windshield into the wind, since the windshield is the glass built to take it and the side windows are not. While it is on your mind, listen for a grind or a squeal from the brakes on the first few stops of the morning. A winter of salt leaves a rust film on the rotors that usually wears off in a block, and if it does not go away, have somebody look at the pads. Do you have a spot under cover for the {vehicle} when a storm comes up?
templates.textBody: {first}, hail season is here, so get the {vehicle} under a canopy when the sky turns green, and if you are caught out, point the windshield into the wind since it is the glass built to take it. Do you have a spot under cover for the {vehicle} when a storm comes up?
templates.editHint: If you know they have a garage, change the question to whether they actually park in it.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — the government recall lookup, which fixes real problems at any dealer for the make
templates.subject: a two-minute recall check
templates.emailBody: One more spring thing, {first}, and it is a quick one. The government keeps a recall list by vehicle, and the lookup at https://www.nhtsa.gov/recalls takes about as long as finding your registration, since all it wants is the VIN off the dash or the door sticker. A recall gets fixed at any {make} dealer at no charge to you, no matter where you bought the rig, and a lot of them are things you would never notice until they mattered. I run my own truck through it every spring and every fall, and I put the date in my phone so I remember. Have you ever run the VIN on the {vehicle} through that lookup?
templates.textBody: {first}, take the VIN off the {vehicle} dash and run it through https://www.nhtsa.gov/recalls because a recall gets fixed at any {make} dealer at no charge. Have you ever run the VIN on the {vehicle} through that lookup?
templates.editHint: If you already ran the VIN at the sale and it was clean, say so and ask if they want you to run it again next spring.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — a driveway road-trip check, including the spare nobody looks at
templates.subject: before the trip up north
templates.emailBody: {first}, before the {vehicle} hauls everybody up north for the Fourth or the cabin weekend, five minutes in the driveway saves a Saturday on the shoulder of Hwy 52. Check the coolant in the overflow bottle while it is cold, look at the tire edges for wear, and then do the one nobody does, which is find the spare and see if it has air. Look under where you park for any fresh drips, and if the temperature gauge has been creeping up in stop-and-go, say so before you tow the boat through it. Toss a gallon of water and a phone cord in the back, since those two cover more roadside trouble than anything else you could pack. Does the spare in the {vehicle} have air in it?
templates.textBody: {first}, before the trip north, check the coolant cold, look at the tire edges, and go find out whether the spare in the {vehicle} actually has air. Does the spare in the {vehicle} have air in it?
templates.editHint: If you know where they go (the cabin, the lake, the in-laws), name the place instead of 'up north'.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — a two-way diagnostic (weak air or warm air) that helps them sort a cheap fix from a shop visit
templates.subject: when the AC is not keeping up
templates.emailBody: {first}, if the AC in the {vehicle} has been blowing cool instead of cold, ask yourself one thing first: is it weak air or is it warm air. Weak air with a musty smell is usually a cabin air filter packed with a year of gravel dust and cottonwood fluff, and that is a ten-minute job behind the glovebox on a lot of rigs. Warm air with decent flow is usually low refrigerant, which means there is a slow leak somewhere, and a can from the parts store just puts it off until the middle of August. Either way it is a known thing, not a mystery, and knowing which one it is tells you whether it is a Saturday morning or a shop appointment. Is it weak air or warm air?
templates.textBody: {first}, if the AC in the {vehicle} is not keeping up, weak musty air is usually a cabin filter and warm air with good flow is usually low refrigerant. Is it weak air or warm air?
templates.editHint: If they mentioned the AC at the sale, open with that instead of the general line.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — heat kills batteries too, and shade is the useful advice nobody gives
templates.subject: heat kills batteries too
templates.emailBody: {first}, everybody worries about a battery in January, but a string of ninety-degree days in a parking lot does more damage than the cold, and the {vehicle} will not tell you until a morning in October when it just clicks. If the posts have that white or green crust on them, a wire brush and a baking soda rinse is a good afternoon job. Keep it in the shade when you can, since a shady spot on a hot day does more for a battery than any gadget. If it is more than four summers old, get it load tested before fall so it is your decision when to swap it and not the battery's. Do you know how old the battery in the {vehicle} is?
templates.textBody: {first}, heat wears a battery down worse than cold does, so if the one in the {vehicle} is more than four summers old, get it load tested before fall. Do you know how old the battery in the {vehicle} is?
templates.editHint: If the battery was replaced at the sale, say so and change the question to whether they park in the shade at work.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — trailer lights, dielectric grease, and crossed chains, the stuff that gets people pulled over on the way to the lake
templates.subject: trailer lights before the lake
templates.emailBody: Boat season, {first}. If the {vehicle} is pulling a trailer this summer, have somebody stand behind it while you run the brakes, blinkers, and running lights, since a dead trailer light is the one thing a deputy on Hwy 58 can spot from a quarter mile. A little dielectric grease in the plug keeps the pins from corroding, and a plug that works in the driveway and quits at Lake Pepin usually just needs the ground wire cleaned. Check the trailer tires too, since they sit all winter and dry rot from the inside, and cross the safety chains under the tongue so it catches the hitch if it ever lets go. Are you pulling a trailer with the {vehicle} this summer?
templates.textBody: {first}, before the first trip to the lake, have somebody stand behind the trailer while you check lights and blinkers, and cross the safety chains under the tongue. Are you pulling a trailer with the {vehicle} this summer?
templates.editHint: If you know they do not tow, skip this one and pick another summer note.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — a dash light decoder that fits in one email, the thing people search for at the side of the road
templates.subject: what the dash lights mean
templates.emailBody: {first}, here is the short version of the dash lights on the {vehicle}, since the owner's manual is buried in the glovebox. Red means stop the engine soon, and the two that matter are the oil can and the temperature gauge, because driving on either one can wreck an engine in a few miles. Yellow means get it looked at, and a steady check engine light is usually a loose gas cap or a sensor, so tighten the cap first and see if it clears in a day or two. A flashing check engine light is the one exception to the yellow rule, and it means stop driving before a misfire turns into a burned-up catalytic converter. Is anything lit up on the dash of the {vehicle} right now?
templates.textBody: {first}, red dash light means stop the engine soon, yellow means get it looked at, and a flashing check engine light means stop driving now. Is anything lit up on the dash of the {vehicle} right now?
templates.editHint: If they told you about a light that is always on (a known TPMS or airbag light), mention it so the note does not sound blind.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — the tire date code, a fact almost nobody knows and everybody can check in the driveway
templates.subject: how old are your tires, really
templates.emailBody: Tires have a birthday, {first}, and hardly anybody knows where to find it. On the sidewall of each tire on the {vehicle} there is a stamp that starts with DOT, and the last four digits are the week and year that tire was made. Rubber goes hard around six years old whether the tread is worn or not, so the tread tells you how much tire is left and the date tells you how much of it is still good. A hard tire is the one that lets go on a hot stretch of Hwy 52 in July or slides on the first glaze in November. Do you know what year the tires on the {vehicle} were made?
templates.textBody: {first}, the DOT stamp on each sidewall ends in the week and year the tire was made, and rubber goes hard around six years whether the tread is worn or not. Do you know what year the tires on the {vehicle} were made?
templates.editHint: If you put new tires on at the sale, say so and change the question to whether the spare is the same age.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — the recall lookup, offered as something Mick does on his own truck
templates.subject: recalls and your VIN
templates.emailBody: {first}, one that is easy to forget until it matters. Carmakers issue recalls all year, not just when it makes the news, and the lookup at https://www.nhtsa.gov/recalls will tell you in a minute whether the {vehicle} has one open, using the VIN off the dash or the door sticker. If it does, any {make} dealer fixes it at no charge to you, no matter where the rig came from. I check my own truck twice a year and it has caught two things I never would have known about. Have you run the VIN on the {vehicle} through that lookup lately?
templates.textBody: {first}, plug the VIN from the {vehicle} into https://www.nhtsa.gov/recalls and any open recall gets fixed at any {make} dealer at no charge. Have you run the VIN on the {vehicle} through that lookup lately?
templates.editHint: If the spring recall note already went to this customer, retire this one for them or change 'lately' to 'since spring'.

templates.principle: Consistency and identity — names their vehicle and their road, so the note could only be about them
templates.subject: how's the {model} doing
templates.emailBody: {first}, I have been wondering how the {vehicle} is handling {hook|the roads out your way}. No agenda here, I just like knowing how the ones I sold are doing once the new wears off. If anything has started rattling, leaking, or lighting up, that is exactly the kind of thing I want to hear about while it is small. Still running good?
templates.textBody: {first}, been wondering how the {vehicle} is handling {hook|the roads out your way}, and if anything has started rattling or lighting up I want to hear about it while it is small. Still running good?
templates.editHint: Fill the hook field before sending; 'the roads out your way' is the fallback, not the goal.

templates.principle: Low-friction reply — asks for a gut answer, not a report, and says so
templates.subject: how the {model} is treating you
templates.emailBody: Hey {first}, it has been a few months since the {vehicle} went home with you, and I am curious how it is treating you on {hook|the drive you do every day}. I do not need a report, just a gut answer. Sometimes people put up with a small annoyance for a year because they figure it is not worth a call, and it almost always is. You know the rig better than anybody now, so I trust your read on it. Any complaints?
templates.textBody: Hey {first}, it has been a few months since the {vehicle} went home with you, and I am curious how it is treating you on {hook|the drive you do every day}. Any complaints?
templates.editHint: Put the actual commute or road in the hook (the Rochester run, the gravel to Goodhue).

templates.principle: Consistency — reminds them what they said they needed and lets them judge whether it is delivering
templates.subject: one question about the {model}
templates.emailBody: {first}, when you bought the {vehicle} you told me what you needed it to do, and I have been wondering whether it is doing it out on {hook|the roads you actually drive}. Nobody knows that answer but you, and it is the only review I care about. If it is falling short somewhere, I would rather know than guess. Is it doing the job you bought it for?
templates.textBody: {first}, you told me what you needed the {vehicle} to do, and I keep wondering whether it is doing it on {hook|the roads you actually drive}. Is it doing the job you bought it for?
templates.editHint: Replace 'what you needed it to do' with the specific job from your notes (towing the camper, the kid's first car).

templates.principle: Low-friction reply — a one-word question that also updates the record if life has changed
templates.subject: still the {model}
templates.emailBody: Quick one from Mick, {first}. I am guessing the {vehicle} is still out {hook|your way} doing its thing, but life changes plans and I would rather ask than assume. If something has shifted, like a kid driving now or a longer run to Rochester, I like knowing that too, since it changes what is worth telling you. Still the {model}?
templates.textBody: Quick one from Mick, {first}, guessing the {vehicle} is still out {hook|your way} doing its thing, but I would rather ask than assume. Still the {model}?
templates.editHint: If you know something changed (new job, new baby), name it instead of the generic list.

templates.principle: Mere exposure — a steady, seasonal, no-ask note that keeps Mick familiar without selling
templates.subject: how the {model} did this {season}
templates.emailBody: {first}, this {season} has been a good test for anything with four wheels, and I keep thinking about how the {vehicle} did on {hook|the stretch you drive every day}. Some rigs surprise people the first year, in good ways and bad, and I like to know which one I handed you. There is no wrong answer, I just want the honest one. Has it been treating you right?
templates.textBody: {first}, this {season} has been a real test for anything with four wheels, and I keep wondering how the {vehicle} did on {hook|the stretch you drive every day}. Has it been treating you right?
templates.editHint: Add one line about what the season actually did (the ice storm, the heat wave) so it is not generic.

templates.principle: Consistency — surfaces the small thing they have been living with, which is how trust gets built
templates.subject: the thing you almost mentioned
templates.emailBody: {first}, here is something I ask everybody once the {vehicle} has a few months of {hook|gravel and highway} on it: I want to know the one thing about it you have gotten used to instead of fixed. Every rig has one, a squeak, a seat that will not quite sit right, a mirror that shakes on the washboard, and people live with it because it does not feel worth a call. It is worth a call. Got one of those?
templates.textBody: {first}, every rig has one thing the driver gets used to instead of fixed, a squeak or a shaky mirror on {hook|the washboard}, and I want to know what the {vehicle} has. Got one of those?
templates.editHint: If they already mentioned a quirk on the test drive, ask about that one by name.

templates.principle: Specific-person referral ask, after giving — the co-worker's kid getting a license, with an explicit 'no is fine'
templates.subject: a kid getting a license
templates.emailBody: {first}, a favor, and a no is a fine answer. The way I get to keep doing this the way I do it, no pressure and straight talk, is by people like you sending me the next one instead of me buying ads. Somebody at your work probably has a kid getting a license this spring and is dreading the whole car thing. If that is a real person, give them my number and I will treat them the way I treated you, which I think you will remember was pretty plain. Anybody at work with a kid about to start driving?
templates.textBody: {first}, favor, and no is fine: if somebody at your work has a kid getting a license this spring and is dreading the car thing, my number is a safe place to send them. Anybody at work with a kid about to start driving?
templates.editHint: Swap 'this spring' for the season it actually is, and 'at work' for wherever they know people (the plant, the school, the co-op).

templates.principle: Specific-person referral ask — the neighbor with the lease ending, framed as mention-my-name, never push
templates.subject: the neighbor with the lease
templates.emailBody: I do not run ads, {first}, so this is how I ask. Somewhere on your road there is a neighbor whose lease is coming due and who is not looking forward to sitting in a showroom in Rochester for four hours. If that person crosses your mind, all I would ask is that you mention my name and let them decide from there, since I would never want you pushing somebody for me. You know how I did it with the {vehicle}, and that is how I would do it with them. Does a neighbor with a lease ending come to mind?
templates.textBody: {first}, I do not run ads, so if a neighbor with a lease ending crosses your mind, mentioning my name is all I would ever ask. Does a neighbor with a lease ending come to mind?
templates.editHint: If they live in town, 'on your road' becomes 'on your block'; if they farm, it becomes 'down the road'.

templates.principle: Specific-person referral ask — the brother-in-law who complains about his truck, asked as a question they can picture
templates.subject: the brother-in-law and his truck
templates.emailBody: {first}, here is a question for the next family supper. There is almost always one person at the table, a brother-in-law or an uncle, who complains about his truck every time it comes up and never does anything about it, and everybody is tired of hearing it. If that is your table, you could send him my way and let me listen to the whole story, because I have found the complaining usually stops once somebody takes it seriously. No pitch from me, just the same conversation you and I had about the {vehicle}. Is there a brother-in-law like that in your family?
templates.textBody: {first}, if there is a brother-in-law at the table who complains about his truck every holiday and never does anything about it, send him my way and I will listen to the whole story. Is there a brother-in-law like that in your family?
templates.editHint: If you met the family at the sale, use the real relation (their dad, their sister's husband).

templates.principle: Specific-person referral ask — someone who just started a Rochester commute, a person they can name in one second
templates.subject: a new commute to Rochester
templates.emailBody: {first}, I have a specific person in mind and you might know them. Somebody at church or in your circle just took a job in Rochester and is about to find out what a daily run down Hwy 52 does to a car that was fine for around-town driving. That person is going to need something dependable before the commute wears the old one out, and I would rather they talk to somebody who will tell them the truth about it. If a name popped into your head just now, pass mine along. Did somebody come to mind?
templates.textBody: {first}, if somebody at church just took a job in Rochester and is about to learn what Hwy 52 every day does to a car, pass my name along. Did somebody come to mind?
templates.editHint: Swap 'church' for wherever this customer actually knows people (the fire department, the softball league, the school).

templates.principle: Specific-person referral ask — the family doing the hand-me-down shuffle, with the outcome left to them
templates.subject: the college kid and the hand-me-down
templates.emailBody: {first}, no pressure on this one, it is just how I keep going without ads. A lot of families around here are about to send a kid off to school with the old car and then quietly realize the parents need something for themselves. If a friend of yours is in the middle of that shuffle, they are welcome to call me and I will talk through it the same slow way I did with you on the {vehicle}. Whether they end up buying from me or not, they will leave knowing more than they came in with. Is a friend of yours in the middle of that shuffle this year?
templates.textBody: {first}, if a friend of yours is sending a kid off to school with the old car and the parents suddenly need something, I will walk them through it the same slow way I did with you. Is a friend of yours in the middle of that shuffle this year?
templates.editHint: In spring, 'off to school' can become 'off to a summer job'; keep the shuffle idea.

templates.principle: Specific-person referral ask — the farmer fighting a worn-out truck, framed as a favor to him rather than to Mick
templates.subject: a truck that quits in harvest
templates.emailBody: Think about who you know that farms or hauls for a living, {first}, and whether one of them spent last harvest fighting a truck that kept quitting when it mattered. Those are the people I like helping, because they know exactly what they need and they do not want to be sold, they want to be listened to. If one of them is grumbling about it over coffee, tell him Mick at Mosaic will hear him out and not waste his morning. You would be doing him a favor more than me. Is there a farmer in your circle fighting a worn-out truck?
templates.textBody: {first}, if somebody you know farms and spent harvest fighting a truck that kept quitting, tell them Mick at Mosaic will hear them out and not waste their morning. Is there a farmer in your circle fighting a worn-out truck?
templates.editHint: In spring, change 'last harvest' to 'planting'; for a town customer, swap the farmer for the guy who plows driveways.

templates.principle: Peak-end plus specific-person referral ask — marks the year, then names the co-worker with the dead car
templates.subject: coming up on a year
templates.emailBody: {first}, you are coming up on a year with the {vehicle}, and I still remember the day it went home. A year is about when people start telling the truth about a car, good or bad, so I hope it has earned its spot in the driveway. Here is the ask: somewhere in your life there is a co-worker whose car quit on them lately and who is dreading the search, and my number in their hand would save them a lot of runaround. That is the whole request, and no is fine. Co-worker with a dead car come to mind?
templates.textBody: {first}, coming up on a year with the {vehicle}, and if a co-worker's car quit on them lately, my number in their hand would save them a lot of runaround. Co-worker with a dead car come to mind?
templates.editHint: Add the one thing you remember from the sale day so 'I still remember' is true on the page.

templates.principle: Specific-person referral ask after a year of giving — the nervous sister or friend, with no obligation attached
templates.subject: almost a year with the {model}
templates.emailBody: Hard to believe, {first}, but you are coming up on a year in the {vehicle}. I still think about that one because it went the way I like them to go, slow and honest, with you making the call and not me. If you have a sister or a good friend who is about to start looking and is nervous about getting talked into something, I would take good care of them, and I would never count it as something you owe me. Just a name and a number passed along, if it fits. Got a sister or a friend about to start looking?
templates.textBody: Hard to believe, {first}, but you are coming up on a year in the {vehicle}, and if a sister or a good friend is nervous about starting to look, my name in their ear would be welcome. Got a sister or a friend about to start looking?
templates.editHint: Swap 'sister' for the relative they actually talked about at the sale.

templates.principle: Consistency plus specific-person referral ask — asks them to picture who is standing where they stood a year ago
templates.subject: a year in, one question
templates.emailBody: {first}, coming up on a year with the {vehicle}, and I want to ask you something honest. Think back to when you were looking, and then think about who you know right now who is standing where you were standing then, maybe a kid at your work with a first paycheck and no idea where to start. If the way I did it with you was worth anything, that person is the one I would want to hear from. You decide whether it fits, and either way, thank you for a good year. Is there a kid at work with a first paycheck and no idea where to start?
templates.textBody: {first}, coming up on a year with the {vehicle}, and if a kid at your work has a first paycheck and no idea where to start with a car, I would want to be the one they call. Is there a kid at work with a first paycheck and no idea where to start?
templates.editHint: If they were the nervous first-time buyer, say 'where you were standing, nervous and all' so it lands.

templates.principle: Mere exposure — a short, human note with nothing attached, so Mick is a person and not a mailer
templates.subject: happy birthday, {first}
templates.emailBody: Happy birthday, {first}. Nothing attached to this one, I just remembered, and a birthday ought to get said out loud. Hope the {vehicle} gets you somewhere good today. Doing anything fun for it?
templates.textBody: Happy birthday, {first}, nothing attached to this one, I just remembered. Doing anything fun for it?
templates.editHint: If you know what they do for fun (the lake, the grandkids), ask about that instead of 'anything fun'.

templates.principle: Mere exposure and low-friction reply — a two-option question anybody can answer from a phone
templates.subject: a birthday note from Mick
templates.emailBody: {first}, I had your birthday written down from when we did the paperwork on the {vehicle}, and I did not want it to go by without saying something. So, happy birthday from Mick at Mosaic, and I hope somebody else is doing the driving today. Cake or pie?
templates.textBody: {first}, had your birthday written down from the {vehicle} paperwork, so happy birthday from Mick at Mosaic. Cake or pie?
templates.editHint: Leave it alone; this one works as-is.

templates.principle: Mere exposure — a reflective line and a one-word question, no ask of any kind
templates.subject: happy birthday
templates.emailBody: {first}, happy birthday from Mick at Mosaic. Another year older means another year of knowing more than you did, which in my experience is the whole point. No ask in this one, just a note from a guy who is glad to know you. Is it a big one this year?
templates.textBody: Happy birthday from Mick at Mosaic, {first}, no ask in this one, just a note from a guy who is glad to know you. Is it a big one this year?
templates.editHint: If you know it is a milestone, say the milestone instead of asking.

templates.principle: Reciprocity, honestly earned — a thank-you with nothing attached and no second ask, sent the day the referral arrives
templates.subject: you sent somebody my way
templates.emailBody: {first}, {referred|somebody you know} came in and said your name, and I want you to know that landed. There is no bigger compliment in this business than somebody trusting you with a friend, and I will treat them exactly the way I treated you with the {vehicle}. Nothing attached to this, no program, no points, just a straight thank you, because you did not have to do that. Whatever happens with them, you did a good thing and I will not forget it. Okay if I tell you how it turns out?
templates.textBody: {first}, {referred|somebody you know} came in and said your name, and that landed, so thank you, nothing attached, I will treat them the way I treated you. Okay if I tell you how it turns out?
templates.editHint: Use the referred person's first name in the first line; check the referred field is filled before sending.

templates.principle: Reciprocity — names the effort it took to refer, and explicitly asks for nothing more
templates.subject: that meant something
templates.emailBody: {first}, I heard from {referred|somebody you sent my way}, and they said you told them to call me. Thank you. I know that kind of thing is easy to not do, and you did it anyway, which says something about how you saw the way we handled the {vehicle}. I am not going to ask you for anything else here, I just want you to know it was noticed. Work friend or neighbor?
templates.textBody: {first}, {referred|somebody you sent my way} said you told them to call me, and I am not asking for anything else here, I just want you to know it was noticed. Work friend or neighbor?
templates.editHint: If you already know how they know each other, change the question to something about the referred person's search.

templates.principle: Reciprocity and identity — reflects back why people refer (protecting a friend), which is the same reason Mick sells the way he does
templates.subject: you did not have to do that
templates.emailBody: You did not have to send {referred|a friend} my way, {first}, and you did. I think about why people do that, and it usually comes down to not wanting a friend to get pushed around, which is the same reason I do this the way I do. So thank you, truly, and there is nothing tied to it. They are in good hands from here. Did they seem nervous about the whole thing?
templates.textBody: You did not have to send {referred|a friend} my way, {first}, and you did, so thank you, nothing tied to it, they are in good hands from here. Did they seem nervous about the whole thing?
templates.editHint: If the referred person already bought, change the last line to a one-word question about how it went for them.

templates.principle: Autonomy respected — instant, no guilt, door left open
templates.subject: you are off the list
templates.emailBody: {first}, you are off the list as of right now, and no hard feelings at all. If you ever need a straight answer about a car, my number still works and I still answer it.
templates.textBody: {first}, you are off the list as of right now, no hard feelings. My number still works if you ever need a straight answer about a car.
templates.editHint: Do not add anything; the whole point is that it is short and asks for nothing.

templates.principle: Autonomy respected — confirms the stop in plain words and leaves the door open without a question
templates.subject: no more notes from me
templates.emailBody: Understood, {first}, that was the last one and you will not hear from me again unless you start it. The door stays open on my end, and I hope the {vehicle} keeps treating you right.
templates.textBody: Understood, {first}, that was the last one from me. The door stays open on my end if you ever need anything.
templates.editHint: Do not add anything; if they gave a reason, do not answer it here.
